summary:
Madrid stands under Spain's national framework for legal gender recognition, with the Comunidad de Madrid's own statute as a layer beneath it. Madrid is one of Europe's principal LGBT urban centres, and the region was among the first in Spain to pass a gender-identity law, adopting its statute in 2016 alongside the Islas Baleares and the Región de Murcia and after Extremadura in 2015. That regional statute was later amended by Ley 17/2023. Regional law must comply with Spain's Ley 4/2023, which sets the statutory floor that a trans visitor's recognition and protection claims in the region rest on.

What the region has withdrawn since then matters to anyone relying on local antidiscrimination machinery. After the 2023 regional election, the new government of the Comunidad de Madrid repealed the region's non-discrimination law, repealed the regional ban on conversion therapy as it applies to trans people, removed the penalties that attached to conversion therapy, and repealed several trans legal recognitions. These measures act on the region's own guarantees and leave the national framework in place.

The safety picture the region's own sources report does not follow from the legal position. Homophobic and transphobic discrimination and violence are described as significant problems in Madrid, and trans people and migrants are reported to face additional barriers within the city's LGBT population.

The community is concentrated and long established. The Chueca district is the centre of the city's LGBT life, and MADO, held annually in late June or early July, is among the largest Pride events in the world and draws millions of attendees. COGAM, founded in 1986, is the city's most influential LGBT organisation; the city government maintains an Oficina de Atención a la Diversidad Sexual y de Género; and Arcopoli works against discrimination and violence.
tangentialFactors: Madrid's place among Spanish regions on this issue is comparatively early. It adopted a gender-identity law in 2016, in the same wave as the Islas Baleares and the Región de Murcia, a year after Extremadura. The region's later narrowing of its own guarantees means that the regional-level protections available to a trans visitor in the Comunidad de Madrid differ from those in force in other Spanish regions, while the national statute applies across all of them.
localsOnly: Residents of the Comunidad de Madrid have their regional recognition and protection claims governed by the region's 2016 gender-identity statute as amended by Ley 17/2023, alongside the 2023 repeals of the regional non-discrimination law, the regional conversion-therapy ban for trans people and its penalties, and several trans legal recognitions. Organisations carrying casework and advocacy locally are COGAM, founded in 1986 and the city's most influential LGBT organisation, Arcopoli, which works against discrimination and violence, and the city government's Oficina de Atención a la Diversidad Sexual y de Género.
outOfScopeNotes: The inventory does not record which regional recognitions the 2023 repeals removed, what the region's 2016 statute provided before Ley 17/2023 amended it, or whether any of the repeals have been challenged. No Madrid-specific enforcement figures, prosecution counts or hate-crime statistics for the region are in the sources, so the reported finding that discrimination and violence are significant problems in Madrid cannot be quantified, and no comparison against a general crime rate for the region is possible from this material. Whether the withdrawn regional conversion-therapy penalties leave any alternative regional remedy is not sourced.
